summary: Security Event Tokens can describe events about many kinds of subjects. This document defines Subject Identifiers as structured JSON objects with named formats. It also creates a registry of such formats, and a JWT "sub_id" claim.

eli5.summary: When reporting an incident, you need to say who it's about, with a name, an email, or a number. This sets up shared name tags so everyone writes them the same way.

questions: subject identifiers for security event tokens
what is the jwt sub_id claim
what identifier formats does rfc 9493 define
subtitle: A common JSON shape for saying who or what a security event is about, with named formats for emails, phone numbers and more.

tldr.problem: Security events and tokens can concern many kinds of subjects, and one subject can be identified in several ways (email, phone number, account, opaque ID), so a receiver needs to know which mechanism is in use.
tldr.mechanism: A Subject Identifier is a JSON object with a "format" member naming an Identifier Format, which fixes the other members. The RFC defines eight formats, a registry for more, and a JWT "sub_id" claim to carry one.
tldr.outcome: Senders and receivers can parse identifying information unambiguously. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 9493 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2023, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines the Subject Identifier formats and the sub_id claim.

sections.title: Why Subjects Need Identifiers
sections.content:
Security events described in Security Event Tokens (RFC 8417) can be about many kinds of subjects, such as a JWT principal, an IP address or a URL. Even for one kind of subject there are several ways to identify it. An account, for example, might be identified by an opaque identifier, an email address, a phone number, or a JWT iss and sub pair.

Different accounts in the same sender and receiver relationship may be identified in different ways, for example when some accounts only have email addresses and others only have phone numbers. So a token needs to say how a subject is being identified. This RFC defines Subject Identifiers as JSON objects, and Identifier Formats as named rule sets for encoding identifying information into them.
sections.eli5: Your friend might be called by a nickname, a phone number or an email. If you tell a teacher about them, you should say which one you are using.

sections.title: Subject Identifiers and Identifier Formats
sections.content:
A Subject Identifier is a JSON object that identifies a subject within some context. It MUST conform to a specific Identifier Format and MUST contain a format member whose value is that format's name. It MUST contain every member the format requires and MUST NOT contain members the format prohibits or does not describe.

Every format needs a unique name, either registered with IANA or a Collision-Resistant Name as defined in RFC 7519. Formats expected to be used broadly SHOULD be registered. The format member is reserved: formats MUST NOT declare rules about it.

Formats say how to encode identifying information, not what kind of thing the subject is. An email Subject Identifier might point to a user, a mailbox or something else both sides understand. Specifications that define formats MUST NOT make claims about the subject itself, such as limiting a format to human users.
sections.eli5: Every name tag has a label on top saying what kind it is. The label tells you how to read the rest, but it does not tell you what the person is like.

sections.title: The Eight Identifier Formats
sections.content:
The RFC defines eight formats, each with one main member that is REQUIRED and MUST NOT be null or empty. Applications SHOULD choose the most specific format. For example, an email address should use the Email format rather than a mailto: URI in the URI format.

  • account: a uri member holding an acct URI (RFC 7565).
  • email: an email member holding an addr-spec that identifies a deliverable mailbox.
  • iss_sub: iss and sub members, like the JWT claims in OpenID Connect ID Tokens.
  • opaque: an id string with no meaning beyond identifying the subject, such as a UUID or a hash.
  • phone_number: a phone_number in E.164 form, with an international dialing prefix.
  • did: a url member holding a DID URL, which may be a bare DID.
  • uri: a uri member with any URI; no assumptions about scheme or reachability.
  • aliases: an identifiers array of one or more Subject Identifiers that all identify the same entity.

Aliases identifiers MUST NOT be nested, and the array SHOULD NOT contain exact duplicates. For email, the RFC notes that providers canonicalize addresses in different, non-standard ways (case, optional dots), so the recipient SHOULD apply its own canonicalization to incoming events.
sections.eli5: There are eight kinds of name tag: email, phone, account and so on. One special tag, aliases, holds several other tags that all point to the same person.

sections.title: The JWT sub_id Claim
sections.content:
The JWT sub claim is a string, so it cannot hold a JSON object. This RFC defines the sub_id claim, whose value MUST be a Subject Identifier for the JWT Subject. It may appear whether or not sub is present. If both are present they MUST identify the same subject, because a JWT has only one subject.

A receiver MUST NOT rely on both claims to determine the subject. It MAY try one and fall back to the other, for example using sub_id first and falling back to sub if the format is not recognized.

A sub_id may hold an iss_sub identifier whose iss and sub differ from the JWT's own. An OpenID Connect client might do this when sending a JWT back to its Identity Provider, to name the subject with an identifier both parties understand.
sections.eli5: The old name slot only fits plain words. The new slot fits a whole name tag, and if both slots are filled they must be about the same person.

sections.title: Privacy: Identifier Correlation
sections.content:
Sending two or more identifiers for one subject together, for example in an aliases identifier or through both sub and sub_id, can reveal more than intended. The receiver learns that the identifiers belong together and may correlate other data on that basis.

A transmitter SHOULD send multiple identifiers together only when the recipient already knows they are related, or when correlation is essential to the use case. The privacy considerations of RFC 8417 (for SETs) and RFC 7519 (for JWTs) also apply.
sections.eli5: If you hand over both a nickname and a home address together, the other person learns they belong to the same kid. Only do that if they need to know.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This specification defines no way to protect the confidentiality or integrity of a Subject Identifier. Where those properties are needed, implementations MUST use what the containing format or another layer provides, such as signing SETs or JWTs with JSON Web Signature, or using TLS at the transport layer.

Further confidentiality and integrity considerations for SETs are in RFC 8417.
sections.eli5: The name tag does not lock itself. If it needs to stay secret or untampered, it has to travel in a sealed envelope.

sections.title: The IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA created the "Security Event Identifier Formats" registry, seeded with the eight formats above. Future entries use the Specification Required policy, and the RFC suggests appointing multiple designated experts. Format names MUST be ASCII lowercase letters, digits, underscores and hyphens, and SHOULD NOT exceed 20 characters.

Reviewers should check that a format is thoroughly documented and that registering it helps interoperability. They should usually not approve a request that would confuse things or duplicate an existing format. IANA also registered sub_id in the JSON Web Token Claims registry.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of name-tag types. New types get added only if they are well described and not just a copy of an old one.
